misconceptions: A child component can change the props it receives
setState changes the state variable immediately
Every value shown on screen should be kept in state

templates.question: What is the difference between props and state in React, and how do you decide where a piece of state should live?
keyPoints: Props are inputs passed by the parent and read-only for the child
State is data a component owns that changes over time; updating it re-renders the component
Values that can be computed from props or state should be computed during render, not stored
State lives in the closest common ancestor of the components that need it (lifting state up)
Data flows down through props; changes flow up through callbacks

templates.question: What is the difference between controlled and uncontrolled form inputs in React, and how would you build a form with validation?
keyPoints: A controlled input takes its value from state and updates it in onChange, so React holds the truth
An uncontrolled input keeps its value in the DOM; it is read through a ref or on submit (defaultValue sets the start)
Controlled inputs make instant validation and dependent fields easy, at the cost of a render per keystroke
Validate on change or blur and again on submit, and show errors next to the fields in an accessible way
Form libraries such as React Hook Form use uncontrolled inputs for performance

templates.question: A search box and a results list are sibling components, and typing in the box should filter the list. How would you structure the state?
keyPoints: Keep the query in the common parent and pass the value and an onChange callback to the search box
Pass the query (or the filtered results) to the list
Compute the filtered list during render instead of storing it in state
Debounce or defer the filtering when it is expensive; keep the query in the URL if searches should be shareable

templates.question: A click handler calls setCount(count + 1) three times, but the counter goes up by only one. Why, and how do you fix it?
keyPoints: A state update is queued and takes effect on the next render
count is the value of the current render, so all three calls set the same next value
The updater form setCount(c => c + 1) computes each update from the latest pending state
React batches the updates of one event into a single re-render

misconceptions: Hooks may be called conditionally when the condition rarely changes
Changing a ref's current value re-renders the component

templates.question: How do useState and useEffect work? When does an effect run, and what is its dependency array for?
keyPoints: useState returns the current value and a setter; calling the setter schedules a re-render with the new value
useEffect runs after React has committed the render to the screen
Without a dependency array the effect runs after every render; with [] once after mounting; otherwise when a dependency changes
The cleanup function runs before the effect runs again and when the component unmounts
Effects synchronise with external systems; values derived from props or state belong in render

templates.question: Why must hooks be called at the top level of a component and never inside conditions or loops?
keyPoints: React identifies each hook by the order in which it is called during render
The state of each hook is stored per component in that order
Calling a hook conditionally shifts the order, so state is matched to the wrong hook
Put the condition inside the hook instead; the ESLint rules-of-hooks rule enforces this

templates.question: A component starts a setInterval in a useEffect with an empty dependency array. The interval callback logs a counter from state, and it always logs 0 although the counter on screen increases. Why?
keyPoints: The effect ran once and its callback captured the counter from the first render (a stale closure)
With an empty dependency array the effect never re-runs to pick up new values
Use the functional updater, keep the latest value in a ref, or list the value as a dependency and restart the interval in the cleanup
The exhaustive-deps lint rule warns about the missing dependency

templates.question: What is useRef used for, and how is it different from state?
keyPoints: A ref holds a mutable value in .current that persists between renders
Changing it does not cause a re-render
It is used for DOM elements (focus, measuring, scrolling) and for values such as timer ids or the latest callback
State is for values that the rendered output depends on

templates.question: Several components fetch data, track loading and error states, and must ignore the response once they unmount. How would you share that logic?
keyPoints: Extract a custom hook that holds the state and the effect and returns data, error and loading
Custom hooks share logic, not state: every component that calls it gets its own state
Abort the request or ignore a late response in the effect's cleanup
A server-state library (TanStack Query, SWR) adds caching, deduplication and retries on top

misconceptions: Effects are the right place to compute derived data
An effect that depends on an object re-runs only when the object's contents change
Fetching in useEffect takes care of caching and deduplication

templates.question: A user page fetches data in a useEffect whenever the userId prop changes. When someone switches between users quickly, the page sometimes shows the wrong user's data. Why, and how do you fix it?
keyPoints: Responses can arrive out of order, so an older request that finishes last overwrites the newer data
In the effect's cleanup set an ignore flag, or abort the request with an AbortController
Only apply a response that belongs to the current userId
Server-state libraries key requests by id and handle this

templates.question: When does an effect need a cleanup function? Give examples, and explain what happens when a dependency is missing.
keyPoints: Cleanup undoes what the effect set up: subscriptions, event listeners, timers, connections, requests in flight
It runs before the effect runs again and on unmount; in development StrictMode React runs setup and cleanup an extra time to expose missing cleanups
A missing dependency makes the effect use stale values and not re-run when that value changes
Objects and functions created during render are new every time, so as dependencies they re-run the effect unless memoised

templates.question: Design how a product list page handles the loading, empty, error and retry states of its API request.
keyPoints: Track the request status explicitly (loading, success, error) rather than inferring it from the data
Show a skeleton or spinner while loading and a distinct empty state when there are no results
Show an error message with a retry action on failure
Keep the previous data visible while refetching, and stop updating state after unmount
Announce status changes to assistive technology

templates.question: Why do many teams use a library such as TanStack Query instead of fetching with useEffect and useState?
keyPoints: Server data is a cache of remote state, not UI state
The library caches by query key, deduplicates concurrent requests and shares the data between components
It refetches in the background, serves stale data while revalidating and retries failures
Mutations can invalidate or optimistically update the cached data
It removes most hand-written effect code and its race conditions

misconceptions: A re-render always updates the DOM
Using the array index as the key is always fine
A child component re-renders only when its props change
The virtual DOM is always faster than updating the DOM directly

templates.question: What is the virtual DOM, and how does React's reconciliation decide what to change in the real DOM?
keyPoints: Rendering produces a tree of React elements, a lightweight description of the UI
On an update React compares the new tree with the previous one (reconciliation)
An element of a different type replaces the old one, and its whole subtree is remounted
An element of the same type keeps its DOM node and component state; only changed attributes are updated and its children are compared
Children in lists are matched by key, and only the computed differences are applied to the DOM in the commit phase

templates.question: What causes a React component to re-render?
keyPoints: Its own state changes to a different value
Its parent re-renders: children re-render by default even when their props are unchanged
A context it reads changes
React.memo skips re-rendering when the props are shallowly equal
A re-render does not necessarily change the DOM

templates.question: In a todo list rendered with the array index as key, deleting the first item makes checkbox states and typed text appear on the wrong items. Why?
keyPoints: Keys tell React which element is which between renders
Removing the first item shifts every index, so React reuses the components and DOM inputs of the wrong items
Use a stable, unique id from the data as the key
The index is acceptable only for static lists that never reorder or change

templates.question: What happens in React's render phase and in its commit phase, and why must rendering be pure?
keyPoints: In the render phase React calls components to compute the new tree and compares it with the old one
With concurrent rendering the render phase can be interrupted, restarted or thrown away
The commit phase applies the DOM changes, then runs layout effects; passive effects (useEffect) run after the browser paints
Side effects during render can run several times or for renders that are never committed, so components must be pure
StrictMode renders twice in development to expose impure components

templates.question: What is automatic batching in React 18, and what do startTransition and useDeferredValue help with?
keyPoints: Several state updates in the same event or tick are combined into one re-render, also inside promises and timeouts since React 18
startTransition marks an update as non-urgent, so urgent updates such as typing are not blocked and the transition can be interrupted
useDeferredValue lets an expensive part of the UI render with a value that lags behind
They make the UI more responsive; they do not make the rendering work itself cheaper

misconceptions: Wrapping everything in useMemo and useCallback makes an app faster
React.memo prevents a re-render even when a new object is passed as a prop
Performance should be optimised before it is measured

templates.question: How do you prevent unnecessary re-renders in React, and when is it worth doing?
keyPoints: Measure first with the React DevTools Profiler
Keep state close to where it is used and split components so an update touches less of the tree
React.memo skips a re-render when the props are shallowly equal
useMemo and useCallback keep object and function props stable so that memoised children can skip
Memoisation has its own cost; use it where renders are measurably expensive

templates.question: A large table wrapped in React.memo still re-renders on every keystroke in the parent's search field, and the profiler says its props changed. What is going on?
keyPoints: The parent creates a new object, array or function prop on every render, for example an inline {} or () => ...
React.memo compares props shallowly, so a new reference counts as a change
Stabilise those props with useMemo or useCallback, or move constant values out of the component
Or move the search state into its own component so that the table's parent does not re-render on each keystroke

templates.question: A dashboard page takes four seconds to become interactive, and scrolling its 5,000-row table is janky. How would you approach optimising it?
keyPoints: Profile first (browser Performance panel, Lighthouse, React Profiler) to find where the time goes
Shrink the initial JavaScript with code splitting and lazy-loading of heavy routes and components
Virtualise the long list so that only the visible rows are rendered
Memoise expensive rows and computations
Load less data up front: paginate, or defer what is not needed for the first view

templates.question: What is code splitting, and how do React.lazy and Suspense support it?
keyPoints: The bundle is split into chunks that are loaded when needed instead of one large download
A dynamic import() creates a split point
React.lazy renders a component from a dynamic import, and Suspense shows a fallback while the chunk loads
Split by route and by heavy, rarely used components; very small chunks add requests

templates.question: A chat window renders every one of thousands of messages and becomes slow as the conversation grows. What would you change?
keyPoints: Rendering thousands of DOM nodes is slow regardless of React
Virtualise the list (for example react-window or TanStack Virtual) so only visible messages are rendered
Give messages stable keys and memoise message components so new messages do not re-render old ones
Load older messages on demand (pagination) instead of all at once

misconceptions: All application state belongs in a global store
Context is a state management library that avoids re-renders
Server data should be copied into Redux

templates.question: When would you use the Context API and when Redux Toolkit for state shared between many components?
keyPoints: Context passes a value down the tree without prop drilling; it is a transport, not a store
Every consumer re-renders when the context value changes
Context suits values that change rarely: theme, current user, locale
Redux Toolkit (or Zustand) is an external store with selectors, so components re-render only when their slice changes, with devtools and middleware
Server data is better kept in a server-state library than in either

templates.question: Several pages need the logged-in user, a shopping cart and the product catalogue. How would you manage each kind of state?
keyPoints: Tell server state from client state
The catalogue is server state: fetch and cache it with a server-state library
The cart is client state owned by the UI: a small store or a context with a reducer, possibly persisted
The logged-in user comes from an auth context or a cached query
Keep state as local as possible and share only what several parts need

templates.question: Every component that reads an AppContext re-renders whenever any part of its value changes, and the app feels sluggish. Why, and how would you fix it?
keyPoints: All consumers re-render when the provided value changes
A value written as an object literal in the provider is new on every render, so it changes every time
Memoise the value with useMemo
Split the context by concern or by how often it changes (for example state and dispatch apart)
For frequently changing shared state use a store with selectors

templates.question: Why is it a mistake to copy props into state, or to store values that can be computed from other state?
keyPoints: A copy goes out of sync: it does not follow later changes of the prop
Two sources of truth for the same fact cause bugs
Compute derived values during render, with useMemo if the computation is expensive
To reset state when an identity changes, give the component a key
